title: A new heaven and a new earth
summary: The finale of the great controversy: sin, death and evil are destroyed forever, and God creates a new heaven and a new earth. No tears, pain or death, with Eden restored and an eternal, close relationship with God - this is the goal of the whole journey and an open invitation.

sections.heading: The end of the great controversy: the end of evil and death

items.comment: After the final rebellion, evil is judged once and for all - Satan, the author of sin, is cast into the fire. The great controversy has an end; evil is not eternal.

questions.text: What peace is there in the thought that evil will not exist forever, but has an appointed end?

items.comment: The text says that death itself and the realm of the dead are destroyed - this is the second death. Nothing is left that could ever wound again.

questions.text: What does it mean to you that one day not only pain but death itself will disappear?

items.label: "the lake of fire / the second death": the end of evil, not eternal torment (Rev 20:10, 14)
items.content: Adventism understands the lake of fire and the second death as the final ANNIHILATION of evil, sin and the unredeemed, and not as eternal conscious suffering. The biblical arguments: death, as the last enemy, is DESTROYED (1 Cor 15:26); the "second death" is precisely a death, not a life in torment (Rev 20:14); and God assures us that affliction will not rise up a second time (Nah 1:9). The effects are eternal (irreversible), but the process is not an endless torture. This keeps the finale consistent with the picture of a God of love and with the promise of a universe free from evil. Exegetical nuances - to be confirmed at review.

items.comment: Paul calls death the last enemy, which will be destroyed. Death is not the natural order, but an enemy - and it will be defeated.

questions.text: How do grief and fear change when you look at death as an "enemy" that is to be removed?

items.label: "He will swallow up death forever": the prophets and Paul speak with one voice (Isa 25:8)
items.content: Paul's image of death as the last enemy (1 Cor 15:26) is rooted in the prophets: Isaiah foretells that God "will swallow up death forever" and "wipe away the tears from every face" (Isa 25:8) - the very same promise repeated in Rev 21:4. Scripture therefore does not treat death as a natural stage, but as an intruder to be removed from God's world forever. This is one of the strongest threads linking the Old and New Testaments in the hope of the new earth.

questions.text: What changes in grief through the awareness that the prophets already saw the day when God Himself will remove death?

items.comment: The prophet assures us that affliction will not rise up a second time. God does not only extinguish evil but guarantees it will never return - the universe will be permanently safe.

questions.text: Why does it matter that evil will be removed once and for all, with no risk of return?

items.comment: The prophet paints a day that will burn up pride and evil, yet for those who worship God it will rise like the sun of righteousness bringing healing. The same day is the end of evil and the beginning of healing.

questions.text: What does it say about God that the very same act ends evil and brings healing to the righteous?

sections.heading: A new heaven and a new earth

items.comment: John sees a new heaven and a new earth in place of the passing, former world. God does not abandon matter - He renews creation, gives a real, physical home.

questions.text: What does it mean that God's future is not an escape from the world, but a NEW, real world?

items.label: "new" as renewed (Rev 21:1, 5; Isa 65:17)
items.content: The Greek adjective used in Rev 21:1, 5 (kainos) usually emphasizes QUALITATIVE newness (renewed, transformed), not merely the next one in a sequence. This fits with Isa 65:17 and with God's declaration of making all things new (Rev 21:5): God does not so much erase creation as cleanse and transform it to the state for which it was intended. The Greek form and its nuance are given cautiously - to be confirmed at review.

items.comment: The heart of heaven is not a place, but a Presence - God will dwell among His people, will personally wipe away every tear and remove death, mourning, crying and pain. This is the end of everything that wounds.

questions.text: Which of these promises - the end of tears, death, mourning or pain - do you most need to hear today?

items.label: "the dwelling of God is with humankind": the goal of all salvation history (Rev 21:3)
items.content: The announcement "behold, the dwelling of God is with humankind" is not one motif among many, but the closing of a thread that runs through all of Scripture: God walking with humanity in Eden (Gen 3:8), the tent of meeting and the temple, "God with us" (Immanuel) - all of it moving toward the moment when God will dwell among His people permanently. The new earth is "the ultimate goal of the gospel and of salvation history." Heaven is, above all, Presence, not scenery.

questions.text: How does the thought that the heart of heaven is God Himself dwelling with you - not a place or rewards - change your understanding of heaven?

items.comment: Isaiah already heard the promise of a new heaven and a new earth, after which former troubles will no longer come to mind. The old pain will torment no more.

questions.text: What would it mean to you that former sufferings "will no longer be remembered" as a wound?

items.comment: The new earth is concrete: building houses, planting vineyards, fruitful work, peace even among the animals, who will no longer harm anyone. This is Eden restored, not a bodiless abstraction.

questions.text: What does it say about God's care that He promises the fullness of life - work, a home, peace - and not just "rest for souls"?

items.label: "from Sabbath to Sabbath": we worship God on the new earth (Isa 66:23)
items.content: Right after the picture of concrete life, Isaiah adds a picture of concrete worship: the saved will come to bow before God "from New Moon to New Moon and from Sabbath to Sabbath" (Isa 66:23). The Hebrew phrase can be understood in two ways - as worship on appointed days (especially the Sabbath as a memorial of creation) or as unceasing worship, "from feast to feast." It seems that the first reading is closer to the original, yet the spiritual richness of the second need not be excluded. Either way, the Sabbath continues on the new earth.

questions.text: What does it say about the Sabbath that, as the one rhythm of worship, it passes unbroken from creation, through all of history, to the new earth?

items.comment: Peter directs our expectation toward a new heaven and a new earth, in which righteousness will dwell permanently. The new world is the environment where good is at home.

questions.text: What would life look like in a world where righteousness "dwells" permanently - nothing twisted, nothing unjust?

items.label: "renewal," not a new creation from nothing (2 Pet 3:13; Matt 19:28)
items.content: The language of 2 Pet 3:7-13 speaks rather of renewal and restoration - of a cleansed universe brought out of the old, not of a second creation "from nothing." This is supported by Matt 19:28, where a term describing the "regeneration" of the world appears (translated as "the new world," "the regeneration"), and by Acts 3:21 - "the times of the restoration of all things." God does not throw His work onto the scrap heap; He redeems it. This is an important argument for the reality and continuity of the new earth. The nuance of meaning - to be confirmed at review.

items.comment: The tree of life returns, and the former curse is removed - this is directly the undoing of the effects of the fall in Eden. History comes full circle: from the lost garden to the regained one.

questions.text: What does it mean that "there will be no more curse" - what weight is then lifted from all of creation?

items.label: Eden restored: the bookends of Scripture (Gen 1-3 to Rev 21-22)
items.content: The closing chapters of Revelation deliberately reverse the effects of the fall from Genesis: the tree of life appears again (Gen 3:22-24 to Rev 22:2), the curse imposed after the fall is removed (Gen 3:17 to Rev 22:3), and God once more dwells with humankind (Gen 3:8 to Rev 21:3). Isa 65:17-25 fills out the picture with the concretes of life (houses, vineyards, peace in nature). The Bible thus forms bookends: from the garden lost to the garden-city regained - this is not an escape from matter, but its redemption. The details of the parallels to be verified at review.

items.comment: The promise to the one who overcomes is relational: God will be his God, and he will be God's child. The goal of eternity is not a reward of things, but closeness with God.

questions.text: Which is the greater promise to you: a perfect world, or that "God will be your God" forever?

items.comment: The saved will see the face of God - what not even Moses could see in this life. A face-to-face relationship, without veils.

questions.text: What would it mean to you to "see God's face" - to live in full, utterly unhindered closeness with Him?

items.label: "they will serve Him": the main occupation on the new earth (Rev 22:3)
items.content: The verb used in Rev 22:3 (latreuo) is a typical word for the worship and service of God - of the same root as those who "washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb" and "serve Him day and night" (Rev 7:14-15). The main occupation of the saved will be the joyful worship of the Lamb. Worship on the new earth is therefore not a duty that interrupts life, but its natural breath - in freedom, face to face with God. The Greek form - to be confirmed at review.

items.comment: The Bible ends not with a threat, but with an invitation: the Spirit and the bride call to come, and everyone who is thirsty may take the water of life freely. The door is open to everyone.

questions.text: Since the water of life is "free" and "for everyone who wishes" - what stands today between you and accepting this invitation?

items.comment: God declares that all is accomplished, and to the thirsty He gives freely from the spring of the water of life. The whole journey through prophecy and the great controversy leads to this gift.

questions.text: What does it mean that the fulfillment of everything is a gift ("free"), and not a reward to be earned?

items.comment: Paul reminds us that what God has prepared for those who love Him has never been grasped by the human eye, ear or imagination. Even the best description of the new earth still cannot match the reality God is preparing.

questions.text: How do you live with hope for something that surpasses everything you can imagine?

items.label: "what the eye has not seen": the description yields to the reality (1 Cor 2:9)
items.content: Paul does not say that we know nothing about the new earth, but that no description can match the reality - "what the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard." E. White comments that the fear of "too material" a picture of heaven led many to "spiritualize" and blur the very truths that let us see in it a real home. We deliberately hold to the concrete: the new earth is a place, not a vague abstraction. Humility ("we cannot grasp it") and the concrete ("it is a real home") go together here.

questions.text: How do you keep the balance between humility before what we cannot grasp and a concrete, real hope of a home on the new earth?

application.text: This is the goal of the whole journey through prophecy and the great controversy: not only the end of evil, but the beginning of the life for which we were created. Sin, pain and death will be removed once and for all - and will never return. God will wipe away every tear and dwell among His people in a real, renewed world: a restored Eden, where the saved will see His face. And the last word of the Bible is not a sentence, but an invitation - everyone who is thirsty may freely receive the water of life. The hope of heaven is not an escape from life - it is the promise of life without end with the One who first loved us.
application.challenge: Write down three things in the present world that hurt you the most, and beside each one note the matching promise from Rev 21:3-4 or Isa 65. Then respond to God's invitation in Rev 22:17 - in your own words tell Him "come" and receive the gift of life.
